newsitem.title: USA: Treasury admits misdoings at U.S. small business fund.
newsitem.headline: Treasury admits misdoings at U.S. small business fund.

text.p: A top administrator at a small business program touted by President Bill Clinton wrote spurious memos to justify loans that had already been made, Treasury Department officials confirmed on Tuesday.
The department's Inspector General concluded that the program's deputy director wrote the documents when he learned that Congress planned to review the program's files, the officials said.

Clinton held up the Community Development Financial Institutions Fund as a model for lending in poor areas, but it has drawn fire from Republicans who charge it made loans to institutions connected to Clinton and his wife Hillary.

House Banking Committee Chairman Jim Leach of Iowa and other senior Republicans on the panel wrote to Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Tuesday saying the memos were part of a plot to deceive a Congressional investigation into the fund's lending practices.

"Senior CDFI officials discussed and implemented a plan that was clearly calculated to mislead the subcommittee on the matter that is at the core of its oversight inquiry -- the process that the CDFI fund followed in choosing the recipients of some $37 million in taxpayer dollars," the lawmakers wrote.
Treasury Department officials later confirmed to Reuters the substance of the Inspector General's report, but maintained that the fund's lending decisions were proper and not politically motivated.

The Inspector General's report, delivered to Congress July 11, found that documents backing loans to four institutions in July 1996 were hastily written the night before Congressional staff planned to review the programs files in April 1997. And contrary to the advice of the program's general counsel, the documents were not dated, the inspector found.
Treasury officials vowed to stand behind the program, while refining its selection process and implementing improved procedures to track and secure documents.

Treasury Under Secretary John Hawke said in a letter to lawmakers investigating the program that the inspector general's report "confirms my strong conviction that the CDFI Fund's decisions with respect to awards were made solely on the merits."

But the Inspector General, Valerie Lau, sent Hawke a follow-up letter reminding him that her investigation had been limited in scope. "The purpose of the OIG's expedited investigation was not the broader issue of whether the CDFI Fund properly or improperly selected which applicants would receive funds," she wrote.

Clinton also touted the program in a closed-door budget meeting on Tuesday with congressional leaders, a White House official said. The program is part of Clinton's urban redevelopment strategy that Congress agreed to fund in its budget agreement with the president, officials said.
Republicans are, however, unlikely to increase the program's funding, as Clinton requested, to $125 million from $50 million last year.

The four loans in question, totaling $11 million, went to Shorebank Corp of Chicago, Illinois, and three related companies. Lawmakers said the college roomate of Hillary Clinton was a high-ranking Shorebank official and that the first lady served on the board of directors of one of the related entities, Southern Development.

Although the Treasury Department found that the three related companies were not "affiliates" of Shorebank, lawmakers noted Shorebank has investments in and exercises broad management control over the three.
